lines.x: Tsk, tsk. The courtroom sure is lively today.
Today's trial will be open to the general public, and broadcasted live. Far too many people will be joining in on the fun.
Heh, this is the first time I've seen jurors representing so many different famiglie arrive in such an orderly fashion. This almost seems more like a press conference than a trial.
After all, the man on trial today is none other than Leontuzzo Bellone.
Signora Sicilia gave the order that 'the famiglie are not to interfere with the new city' but didn't elaborate on her plans beyond that. Everybody's scratching their heads.
Finally, the court representing Signora Sicilia's will is about to make its move, so of course it has everyone's undivided attention.
But, the woman adjudicating the trial is that Judge Lavinia, and everybody knows she's tied up with the Bellones.
There's no Bellones anymore, they're stricken from the books. What kind of connections could she have?
If you ask me, she's taking the initiative to convict Leontuzzo, exactly because she wants to show everybody she's done with the Bellones.
And besides, Signora Sicilia's made it pretty clear what she's up to here. She's gonna make an example of him.
She's playing her cards well.
Who knows.
Anyways, since Bernardo was the mastermind behind everything, his son's obviously involved. Today's trial should give us the closure we're looking for.
Fair enough.
Look, the judge is here.
Order in the court.
Presumably, many of you are perplexed about today's hearing.
That is to be expected, because while you may know the man on trial today, you do not know the contents of the case.
I ask that you all remain patient.
I trust that nobody has forgotten that day, one week ago.
So much happened. Minister Rubio's broadcast, and the ensuing chaos that engulfed the city.
Many people died during that turmoil, and many others had their lives turned upside-down.
Fortunately, it was all eventually smoothed over.
Many people know now that Bernardo Bellone, the man who instigated this chaos, lost his life to it as well.
Yet his objectives, as well as his motives, remain mysterious.
During that incident, another man played an important role. He is none other than Bernardo Bellone's son, Leontuzzo Bellone.
Bring him forward.
Order, order.
For some of you, this may be your first time seeing me. For others, you might've known me for a long time.
But first, allow me to introduce myself. I am Leontuzzo Bellone, and I am just an ordinary civilian now.
Ordinary civilian? Aren't you the heir to Famiglia Bellone?
I was. But now, I do not belong to any famiglia.
I know you all have many questions, and I will answer them one by one. First and foremost, however, I must explain what my father did, and how it came to this.
All of this most likely began with the death of Carracci, Ministero dei Lavori Pubblici.
Leontuzzo, standing at the center of the courtroom under the watchful eyes of the entire crowd, shows no signs of nerves at all.
He methodically lays out the backdrop to this entire incident, starting from the assassination.
The other famiglie seem to have already received the news about the ownership of the new city.
I know. 'The famiglie are not to interfere with the new city.'
That she's willing to hold down the other famiglie is proof she wasn't lying when we talked.
But as far as I know, she neither said who would manage the new nomadic city, nor did she explain her rationale.
That's how Grey Hall has always worked.
Signora Sicilia doesn't need to explain everything. Her orders are absolute.
But, we need her explanation.
Right now, everything about the new city is shrouded in uncertainty, and we owe the people an explanation.
That's right, which also brings us to our first dilemma.
Everything happened so suddenly. Am I supposed to get up on stage and announce to everyone, 'hey, we're going to build a city without famiglie?'
That would only scare everyone away.
If the only ones who end up there are you, me, Cellinia, and Rubio's followers, we've already failed at the very first step.
I'm guessing Signora Sicilia wants to see how we handle this.
Looks like you have something in mind.
I do.
I want you to arrest me, Lavinia.
Come again?
My father's actions, no matter his motivations and intentions, put us in this mess.
Someone must be held accountable, in the eyes of the people.
But...
Besides, I'm doing the same thing, aren't I?
The assassination of Carracci, the alliance with the Saluzzos, the assassination of Donna Rossati, and finally, the separation of the secondary core area.
Though some of these events were not secret, when people learned that Bernardo was the driving force behind them, a commotion still broke out in the courtroom.
Leontuzzo lays out his father's plan as objectively as possible using the information he has.
Finally, after an hour-long exposition, the story comes to an end.
I know that many of you are here on behalf of various famiglie, and I assume you've all heard a number of rumors.
That one rumor is correct.
Everything was my father's doing, and the reason why he did it was––
'For a Siracusa without famiglie.'
How is it possible that the don of a famiglia would want to tear down the entire system?
Good question. Even I, his own son, was shocked when I found out.
This idea took root in my father's heart decades ago. And it only just now bore fruit.
Leontuzzo, drop the act already. Your father's dead, but you're still here. That's why you're trying to clear your name with all this nonsense.
After all, we know exactly who the new city belongs to.
I can handle accusations from some famiglie associates or soldiers, if that makes you happy.
If he was the mastermind behind all this, then why did he end up dead?
Il Signore dei Lupi.
Leontuzzo almost blurts the words, but finally suppresses them within his heart.
Because, everything about that existence is utterly absurd.
My father believed that if famiglie should not exist, then he should be eliminated too.
So, after setting everything in motion, he chose to commit suicide.
Pretty damned good joke there, kid!
You're telling me he was such a selfless saint? He really did all this for the common Siracusan?
The exact opposite, actually.
My father was solipsistic, if anything. Everything he did was for the sake of the painting in his memory he called Siracusa.
Which is why he failed.
Alright... I get it now.
Hah, no wonder. That's why Bernardo's dead, and you're still alive.
I dunno what kind of stunt you pulled, but you somehow stopped your papa, and then went to Signora Sicilia and took credit for it.
That's how you got yourself the right to manage the new city. And now, you're up here spinning a magical tale for us, trying to win some sympathy for yourself.
Isn't that right, you patricide?
Leontuzzo lets out a deep sigh, but in the end, looks away without refuting the accusation.
Deep down, he cannot deny it.
Look at that, see the guilt on his face!
I have a question.
Even if we did believe all that garbage, Your Honor, what does it have to do with the trial?
It's not like you want us passing judgment on a dead man and handing down a sentence for his crimes?
Because Leontuzzo is not here as a witness to tell you about his father or opine about his actions.
The case being heard today concerns the ownership of the new city.
Leontuzzo arbitrarily determined what is to come in this new city, and in Siracusa as a whole.
Leontuzzo, please explain to us why Signora Sicilia chose you.
I was both my father's accomplice in everything that happened, as well as the one who stopped him.
I became the latter after I learned the truth.
I believe that my father was misguided, and that his actions would not bring a new era to Siracusa.
Even if dragging all the famiglie into a war would somehow see them erase each other in the end, it does not necessarily mean that the people would choose a new way of life.
But beyond that, I saw a real opportunity in all this.
So, at the end of everything, I went to Signora Sicilia and asked to borrow a city from Siracusa.
'A city without famiglie.'
Another joke? Why would Signora Sicilia ever agree to that?
Because it wasn't actually a request. It was a challenge to Siracusa.
In Signora Sicilia's eyes, my father's methods violated her order, and she couldn't tolerate that.
But the method I chose... Though I don't want to put it this way, was something she found permissible. Otherwise, I wouldn't even be standing here speaking to all of you.
Leontuzzo looks in a certain direction, to where a Sankta priest is standing.
The blindfolded priest does not seem to be paying attention to the ongoing trial.
Alright. If what you say is true, then Signora Sicilia's order does make more sense...
Or I guess, this is the only explanation for why Signora Sicilia would've decided that.
If this really is true, Leontuzzo, then everything you're doing today is just for show.
Call this a trial? You might be standing here, this is all just announcing you as owner of the new city. Isn't that right?
No, this city does not belong to me.
The new city will have everything you'd expect it to, with one exception—famiglie.
You really think you can keep them out?
What a stupid question. It's just as if I asked you, has the boundary between famiglie and ordinary civilians ever been respected?
Famiglie are only willing to abide by Signora Sicilia's rules because she's strong enough to dominate them.
And this gentleman's agreement among famiglie only exists because they don't have what it takes to wipe each other out.
Of course you'll come to the city. I know that, obviously.
But this time, you'll see what it is you've always underestimated.
Of course, I will welcome any famiglie looking to bring change as partners in the new city.
I don't think there's any difference between 'a city without famiglie' and 'Siracusa without famiglie.' They're both crazy.
Do you say that because it's unrealistic, or because it's hard?
Because it's unrealistic, of course.
My father was definitely misguided, but I don't think either of these ideas are unrealistic.
You're just too used to letting your eyes decide what is and is not realistic.
The famiglia are deeply ingrained into this land. You can't hope to uproot them. Nobody can.
But famiglie can be changed, and they can become more civilized.
Even if they can't be wiped out, they should be changed into something else. And as long as that something else is what we want, then that's fine too.
And you really think you can make that work?
I might fail, but don't you think it's worth a shot?
The only thing you've won for yourself is a handout from Signora Sicilia.
The famiglia system still exists. Though it may appear shaky right now, it is by no means so easy to topple.
No matter if this business today is serious or just for show, it's only possible because you have Signora Sicilia's permission.
Is there actually any point to all of this?
Unfortunately, if things don't pan out the way I want them to, then I'm afraid we'll simply be replaced like a tablecloth.
Plus, I've never considered my success inevitable. That day, I was honestly ready to die.
But that doesn't mean I won't take an opportunity that presents itself, handout or not.
Maybe in some other place, given the same set of circumstances, someone in my position could've been a better person and turned down the handout.
But in Siracusa, at this very moment, if this is the only way to move things forward, then that is the pill I will swallow.
Would Ministro Rubio have done what he did, if there was another option?
Are you aware of the consequences?
No.
What we're doing is unprecedented. How am I supposed to guess what the consequences will be?
But, this is what I believe.
Lavinia, I owe an answer not only to all of Volsinii, but to you and everyone around you. Right?
After that day, we didn't get a chance to talk things through, and only had a vague idea of what the other was thinking.
Are we really walking down the same path?
Is the new city that I want the same as the one you want?
We don't really know how the other thinks, do we?
...I trust you.
If you trust me, that's all the more reason to pass judgment on me.
Not just for your sake, but for all the officials who've rallied around you because of Rubio.
Otherwise, what reason would they have to trust me, a man who was mafia royalty?
This isn't a burden you have to carry alone.
I ought to shoulder the responsibility with you.
No... I've finally come to understand the words you said to me, Lavinia.
Our world views are fundamentally different.
As the former heir to a famiglia, there's no way I can empathize with your perspectives and experiences.
What I have to suffer now... is just dealing with whatever's left over after unloading that identity.
Also, from a utilitarian perspective, the people trust you, and this is a real chance for you to lock in that image.
If you put it like that, I'm afraid a lot of people will see this trial as nothing more than a show.
Let them think that then. It doesn't matter.
Even if they do think it's a show, sometimes, the willingness to put on a show is already a gesture in its own right. Don't you think?
Anyway, Lavinia, that's what I think.
We haven't accomplished anything big just yet.
One day, we'll end up mistrusting each other.
One day, when we come to our senses, we might realize that we've been misguided all along.
But...
Leontuzzo Bellone, what is it that makes you stand here so resolutely?
You were born into a famiglia, yet now, you've become the famiglie's worst enemy. Why?
Why, huh... I ask myself the same question a lot.
Is it my idea of chasing efficiency?
Was I raised on ideals of justice?
Is it because of the actions of an admirable government official?
Is it a conclusion from a minor observation of changes in the famiglie?
Maybe all of the above.
If we put all these reasons together, we might be able to come up with an answer––
The time has come.
Maybe Carracci avoided assassination and became a successful Ministero dei Lavori Pubblici, working hard towards a similar goal.
Maybe Ministro Rubio chose to show restraint and continued to occupy his position, secretly winning people over with his lofty ideals and striving to bring change to Siracusa.
This wasn't some elaborate plan I've been hatching my whole life. It suddenly dawned on me at some point, and I only made it this far on luck.
If I die, there'll be someone who comes after me, and another man after that.
And none of this is a testament to how hard I work or how unique I am. It just means that––
The time has come for Siracusa to change.
One question after another is thrown at Leontuzzo, the entire court filled with voices interrogative and vitriolic.
He stands in the center of the courtroom, earnestly and tirelessly answering every question he deems worthwhile.
Slowly but surely, more and more people begin to think that this young man is actually quite thoughtful, and that––
He's serious.
In the end, the courtroom's entire atmosphere seems to cower before him.
All the jurors present, all the civilians watching, and all the people tuning in through various media.
Until now, my heart has been filled with uneasiness.
I borrowed this city from Signora Sicilia, but never saw it as something that belonged to me.
I borrowed this city from Signora Sicilia so we could work together to build something completely new, for all of you to work towards a Siracusa free from the famiglie.
Because I made that decision on everyone's behalf, I must also face everyone's judgment.
But, if you'll let me make a single grand statement–
At this moment, Siracusa doesn't have the right to judge me.
And so, I can only be judged... by all of you.
You will receive this right, just as if you had won the power to build an entirely new city.
Maybe one day, at one point in the future, the power to determine Siracusa's future will also lie in your hands.
This new city welcomes all of those dissatisfied living under the yoke of the famiglie and those who have their doubts, including doubts about me.
That's all I wanted to say.

lines.st: The trial, believed to be Leontuzzo's first public speech as Nuovo Volsinii's mayoral candidate, sparked widespread discussion as well as heated resistance from some famiglie.
But without a doubt, this one-man show of a trial at long last laid the foundations for Nuovo Volsinii to truly come into fruition.
It is but a new beginning.

recs.name: Double-Edged Sword
recs.tag: Looking back on it, he had every idea what was going on.

lines.x: The shady undercurrents flow beneath the clamor of Carnevale. Yet Leontuzzo, in his coma, is unaware of any of this.
Leontuzzo has a dream.
In his dream, he recalls his long-forgotten past.
The central figure of this dream is neither his mentor and friend, Lavinia, nor his close companion Demetri, nor even his father, Bernardo.
It is not Carracci, who guided him with such a steady hand, nor is it Rubio, who startled the entire city with a single gunshot.
It is an old man.
An old man that Leontuzzo has buried in the deepest recesses of his memory.
Back then, the Grey Hall had just passed the resolution to construct a new nomadic city.
Back then, Lavinia had not yet arrived in Volsinii, and he, following his father's orders, took over the 'family business'.
Back then, Siracusa's rainy season was still a long one.
I hereby find Enzo... not guilty!
Not guilty?! He ripped out my sister's vocal chords! Julia is still in a coma!
There is no evidence directly implicating him.
Of course not! He destroyed the evidence!
And he assaulted me!
According to the witnesses' testimony, you were the one who provoked the conflict, and his actions should be considered self-defense.
However, Enzo has said he understands your anger and will not take action against you, either criminally or civilly, in this matter.
You mean, he forgives me?
You are Julia's brother, so you're my brother as well.
We need to maintain a good relationship, Ennio.
You, you bastardo! I never liked you from the start!
Julia insisted on being with you, so I reluctantly agreed.
And look what happened! You've made her a mute!
I already told you. That has nothing to do with me.
She fled back home!
As her boyfriend, I'm very upset about this myself.
Don't worry. After I bring her back to our home, I'll get some of my boys together and we'll go find the real culprit!
No. I won't let you take her away.
Signori, what is the meaning of this?
We're here for a pickup.
But court is still in session.
Then let's wrap it up quick.
We're here to take Julia home.
Well... in that case...
Wait.
Leontuzzo?! So the Bellone Underboss has made an appearance.
Regardless of the circumstances, Julia did flee back home.
She should be allowed to rest quietly until she wakes up.
Even if Enzo is her boyfriend, he should only be allowed to visit her.
I won't allow him to set foot in my home!
Ennio, don't get carried away.
If Signor Bellone hadn't spoken up, your pastry shop would be a pile of ashes by tomorrow!
You—
Ennio, please respect the court's ruling.
Yes... Your Honor.
Enzo, do you accept Signor Bellone's proposal?
The Bellone Underboss has spoken. Of course I accept.
After we're done here in court, I'll go to see her.
Well then, this concludes our proceedings here today.
Buongiorno, Signor Bellone.
Buongiorno, Judge Russo.
Lavinia misses you very much.
I have the letter she sent me. It seems she has a good relationship with Famiglia Bellone.
You are not satisfied with the outcome here in court today.
Enzo is behind this. Everyone can see that.
I know what you mean.
However, he has destroyed all the evidence.
Enzo has some complicated famiglia connections.
This is the most I can do, given the circumstances.
Lavinia tells me you are a man who does not tolerate injustice.
Times have changed, Signore.
People can change as well.
Now, if you don't mind, I shall take my leave.
I still have some matters to attend to. Ennio must be quite upset right now, and I need to go talk him through it.
As you wish.
Ever since the Grey Hall announced the construction of a new nomadic city, Volsinii has been in chaos.
As you've just seen, the courts stopped functioning a while ago.
Judge Russo is one of the few judges in Volsinii who's still got the balls to hold trial.
I know.
Then when do you plan to come back?
Don't you think it's odd for Enzo to be so public about searching for his girlfriend?
This isn't some 'lovers' quarrel'—it's clearly more than that.
He's very impatient.
Are you saying that Julia knows something she isn't supposed to know?
And he won't let it go.
Enzo is with Famiglia Stracci, and they've been causing trouble lately. You've been wanting to make a move against them, right?
Looks like Leon isn't planning on playing the righteous hero. Funny enough, I got some interesting news of my own.
Hmm?
There's an old folk legend among the civilians in Volsinii.
Over the years, many mafiosi who testified in court have met untimely deaths.
The civilians say it's 'divine punishment'.
Well, is it?
Hardly.
The deaths of these people, while somewhat peculiar, are nothing more than assassinations by rival famiglie.
There's no chance someone is pulling strings behind the scenes?
They would need a thorough understanding of all famiglia dynamics, as well as the ability to leave no trace of their existence.
I doubt such a person exists in Volsinii.
Perhaps you're right.
They're getting ready to make a move. We'll talk about this later.
Heh. I never expected the Bellone Underboss to show up there.
Whatever, as long as I can still see Julia.
What really happened between you two?
Nothing, just a misunderstanding. You should head back now. I'll go find Julia.
Tell the Don I'll explain it to him when I get back.
Good. Glad you understand it's on you to explain it to the boss.
*sigh*
Well, I better go to Julia before I see the Don...
You're ditching your wingman.... interesting.
After I see Julia, I'll need her to...
Hey! Outta my way!
That's.... an Iberian outfit?
Guh—
Go to hell!
What is this, a mob hit? I better stop—
Stop!
But—
We're here to take him back alive.
Just leave him to me.
Alright...
It seems you guessed wrong, Demetri.
Ouch—
What happened to me...?
I remember I was going to look for Julia... in the park, when I was jumped by some weirdo in strange clothes... and then...
They knocked me out!
But where am I now? Did someone rescue me?
You will die here.
Who, who are you?
You're really gonna kill me?! I'm a Stracci!!
Famiglia Stracci?
You colluded with the Saluzzos to sell the Straccis' stockpile of Originium weapons.
Your boss is looking for you. I bet he wants to ask you about that, no?
Is Julia up yet?!
Poor Julia. She stumbled upon your business with the Saluzzos, so you tore out her vocal chords.
She was planning to rat me out.
I'm not out to kill her. I still love her.
You dare claim you love her?!
You're... Ennio?! Yes, you've gotta be Ennio!
I get it. You're upset, and you got a bunch of people together to 'scare' me, right? This is all some kinda show?
No. You will die here today.
Do you understand what you're saying here, pal?
Of course.
Your Honor, if you will.
You people are crazy. You're all nuts!
A judge has the power to convict, but not the right to personally take a life.
Moreover, based on what I just heard—there still seems to be some 'wiggle room' in regards to Enzo's sentence.
Am I right, Judge Russo?
Now's the chance—
No one said you could leave, Enzo.
Guh...
You never cease to surprise me, Signor Bellone.
The surprising one here is you, Your Honor.
You really had me fooled with your 'professionalism'.
I never suspected that, behind the scenes, you hold the law in complete disregard.
Your actions make you utterly unworthy to wear a robe and hold a gavel.
But, Leontuzzo, when have rulings against the Siracusan famiglie ever truly followed the law?
No one cares about the evidence.
No one cares about the outcomes.
I won't let this happen.
Say what you will, but I have seen these things countless times.
Moreover, if one crime isn't enough to warrant death, what about ten? Or a hundred?
Mafiosi love to talk of their opulent famiglie.
But how many civilians have bled for this opulence? How many skeletons are there in the closet?
Are these sins not worthy of capital punishment?
Following your logic, every mafioso should be killed.
Yes, and what of it?
Sorry...
But I can't let you kill him.
No one has the right to take another's life.
One judge who ignores the law... paves the way for a lawless future for countless others.
'The future'? Look around you, young Leontuzzo.
Siracusa has no future!
It does indeed. It's merely obscured by Signora Sicilia, the Dodici Famiglie, and this torrential rain.
Even if Lavinia had the ability to influence you, she could never shake your foundation—everything you've been exposed to as a Don's heir—
Systemic violence, deep-seated arrogance, and pretentious hypocrisy.
However, you, Signore, you seem to be different.
You genuinely believe in the existence of justice.
You, an heir to a famiglia, are standing here to uphold the dignity of the law.
Do you understand? This is—
Nothing less than the greatest insult to people like us.
Hmph, I'll have to retreat, with Enzo, for now.
Damnit! Where did he go?!
Sorry, Signor Bellone.
If I stay here, these guys are gonna kill me, but if I go back to the famiglia with you...the Don will kill me!
I don't wanna get killed.
Merda! That judge is off his rocker!
How dare you lay hands on a made man?!
If Leontuzzo hadn't stepped in, I would have been dead meat.
Alas, I must apologize to you, Signor Bellone.
I sincerely appreciate you saving me from that evil judge, but you already know about my betrayal.
Going back with you is no different than jumping off a bridge.
But then, what should I do?
Go hide with the Saluzzos?
They might not even think I'm worth their time... wait!
Ratting out Judge Russo would generate massive headlines!
Just think of it! A bunch of civilians killing mafiosi right under the dons' noses!
The balls on these pricks!
Come to think of it, there must have been some Saluzzos killed too.
I'm sure they'll wanna know about that!
Signor Bellone...
Calm down, Ennio.
I come not for revenge, nor to ask you about Judge Russo.
I just have one question for you.
Which is...?
Why do you trust Judge Russo?
You're a leader in your famiglia, and an honorable one at that. I can tell.
I want to trust you.
But you live in a different world from me.
Even if what you say is true, I will never see it play out, nor will my sister.
I know how the famiglie get their revenge. They send presents to your doorstep: a hand, a foot, maybe an ear or two.
If that is the only way justice is served, then at least...
I want to see it with my own eyes.
After our first meeting, Judge Russo took me to meet some people.
Those people... are just like me.
I'm going to go meet with them again now.
Can I come with you?
If you wish.
He follows Ennio to a restaurant, where people are already waiting.
Most of them wear a look of grief, and some have visible disabilities.

When they see Leontuzzo following Ennio, they do not react much. They simply move the tables aside, arrange the chairs into a circle, and begin taking their seats one after another. Ennio sits down with them.
Leontuzzo stands at the entrance, silently observing the entire scene.
Today, we gather to share our sorrows with our friends.
I'll go first.
My sister discovered that her boyfriend, a mafioso, was secretly smuggling goods with other famiglie, and as a result, her vocal cords were destroyed.
My daughter tried to take her own life on numerous occasions at home. I had to tie her down. Her abuser shows no signs of remorse. In fact they are still trying to take her away from me.
My little brother...
The victims share stories of terrible things that have happened to them or people around them.
Some people are angry, others are crying, and others are almost too pained to speak.
Yet, they console one another, like brothers and sisters.

Our dear friends and family, or even ourselves, have suffered injustice at the hands of the famiglie—some have died, some have been gravely injured, and others have been left with scars that will never heal.
We are hurt, we are enraged, but there is nothing we can do about it.
No. Judge Russo has given us hope!
That's right. In our moments of despair, it was Judge Russo who told us that we are NOT powerless.
Judge Russo told us that we should not lose faith in the law; what we should hate are the villains who trample on it.
Judge Russo told us that he would uphold the law and seek justice on our behalf.
Yes. Judge Russo will punish the villains for us!
Because the law must be just!
Because our anger is righteous.
Because the mafiosi should be punished for their sins!
It's me.
There is something that I think I should tell you.
The Saluzzos just sent a crew to the courthouse.
What?
According to our informant, it seems Enzo was spotted at a Saluzzo base.
Tsk.
You're going to the courthouse, yes?
Yes.
I knew it. I was afraid you'd act on impulse.
But, tell me why, Leon.
This involves the Saluzzos. It's no longer just your business.
You are the Underboss.
Yes, and I want to remain worthy of the title.
In that case, do whatever you think is best.
You wanted to speak with me, Your Honor?
Yes. The famiglie have been growing more and more ruthless these days.
I've decided to give the employees of the court a vacation.
R-Really?
Yes. Pass the message along. Everyone who is still at work can return home.
Alright...
Are there other matters to discuss?
Yes. Several.
Signor Bellone...
He looks at the old man standing before him. The old man is no longer as calm as when they first met, nor as passionate as he had been the night before.
The old man just looks... tired.
Don't you hate me?
Why would I hate you?
Famiglia Saluzzo is coming for you.
If only I hadn't let him get away—
If it wasn't this Enzo, it would have been the next Enzo.
His double-dealing is just more proof of this country's hopelessness.
I think we have all gotten used to it by now.
But you, Signore,
You could have enjoyed your victory in peace. Why are you taking the risk of coming to see me now?
I followed Ennio and saw a support group for victims of the famiglie.
I'm a victim too.
Sixty years of loyalty, and what did I get for it? A package at my doorstep... containing my wife's bloody hand.
That's when I became one of them.
But... from what I've seen...
You're just acting as their hitman.
To uphold the dignity of the law, and to ensure that those victims who have lost faith in the famiglie do not lose faith in the law—
You have made a wicked bargain with the victims, signed in blood.
You have far exceeded the bounds of the law.
I don't believe that everything happening now is what you originally intended.
Whether they coerced me or I raised my blade of my own accord, for their sake, it makes no difference here in Siracusa.
But you, Signore,
What are you planning to do?
Did you come here to see me repent...
Or to extend your hand in charity?
You old fool, I'm here to avenge the mafiosi you murdered!
Enzo, I'm impressed by your ability to adapt to your situation.
(hushed voice) Signor Bellone....?!
This has nothing to do with you, Signor Bellone.
I am here on behalf of Famiglia Saluzzo. I shall avenge the countless mafiosi that have died by this bastardo's wicked, bloody hands!
As for the misunderstandings between us, we shall discuss those later.
So, you've got the Saluzzos backing you now.
Y-yes. What of it?!
That's good then.
What are you doing?!
Demetri.
You called?
Tie them all up. Then go give my regards to the Saluzzos. Ask them to send someone a bit higher up the food chain.
At once.
What are you planning, Signor Bellone?
I will give you two options.
The first option is to reopen Enzo's case. This time, I'll be present, and so will associates of Famiglia Saluzzo.
I guarantee the trial will be safe.
The second option: leave this place.
Out of respect for the law, I will escort you to the city gates, but beyond that, we cannot guarantee your safety.
You are serious about this?
Of course.
I also guarantee that the judgment you issue will be carried out.
Then, obviously, I pick the first option.
Even if I were to die immediately after this trial, I would gladly choose this option.
You will not die. Otherwise, I wouldn't know how to explain all this to Lavinia.
You need to give her a message from me—
In the future, if and when she travels to Volsinii, the Bellones will protect her, as always.
Now, go prepare to reopen the case.
You never told me about this. My teacher never told me about this.
Back then, telling you would have only hurt you.
Judge Russo was planning to tell you, before his death.
But I told him I'd tell you when the time was right.
You picked a good time, indeed.
I know you were worried that when I woke up, I would be devastated by everything that happened during Carnevale.
But I sincerely mean it when I say—
I feel grateful, Lavinia.
You see, history repeats itself.
Back then, Volsinii was dangerous and chaotic.
Amid the fighting famiglie, no one cared about the lives of the ordinary people, and so Judge Russo became a blade of vengeance.
And now, although Nuova Volsinii has its flaws, the implementation of the 'New Urban Management Act' has been highly effective.
Admittedly, in areas we overlooked, Irene came close to making a foolish decision—
But that was merely a close call.
I'm relieved to hear you feel that way.
We all know that many things have changed.
All we need to do is try a little harder... that's all.
